name: Beth Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on at seven, so I'm in by quarter to, counting floats for six tills and checking who's called in sick. I'm the team lead on the front end, so I juggle breaks, cover the cigarette kiosk and sort out every price that scans wrong. The bit I like is the regulars, like the old man who buys one lemon every single day and tells me the football scores. What wears me out is standing nine hours and being the one who says sorry for things head office decided.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You mentioned head office deciding things. What's changed at the store lately?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Last spring they put in ten self-checkouts where four staffed tills used to be. I'm the one who walks between them all day approving beer and unsticking the bagging area. My hours didn't drop, but two of the girls on my team went from thirty hours to twenty, and nobody asked us anything first. I've been in the shop workers' union since I was nineteen, and that was the first time I really used it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say at the staff canteen: the tech was never the problem, the bosses are. If AI turns out to be a damp squib, fine, but they'll still find a way to cut hours. Online I'd probably share something from the union about staffing levels and leave it at that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means my life stays as tight as it is now. Me and Tom (my partner) have about two weeks of money in the bank, and the rent on our terrace went up forty a month in September. Nothing radical changing isn't the same as nothing to worry about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job well and keep pushing at union meetings for minimum hours in contracts. I'd try to put twenty a week aside, which I've said every year and never managed. I wouldn't touch any AI stuff, because I don't need it to run six tills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved for about a minute, then just tired. It's the same treadmill, the same worry when the boiler makes a noise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the bosses would still find ways to cut hours. Where would that hit you first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably my overtime, which is the only reason we cover the rent some months. If they trim my Saturdays, that's about a hundred and twenty a month gone. I know exactly which week that hurts: the one when the car insurance comes out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your team would you worry about most in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Janet, who's done twenty-two years on the tills and can't stand the self-checkouts. She's the first one they'd ease out, because she's slow on the screens and she's expensive. I'd fight for her, but I've seen how that goes.

say: The **bosses** cut hours whether AI works or not, so blaming the **technology** misses the point.
I'd share **union** posts about proper **staffing levels** rather than argue about AI.
think: With about **two weeks** of savings, my life stays **tight** even if nothing changes.
Losing my **Saturday overtime** would cost about **£120** a month, which is the rent gap.
do: Push at **union meetings** for guaranteed minimum hours in every contract.
Try to **save £20 a week**, a goal I've missed every year so far.
Keep running the tills the same way and **avoid AI tools** altogether.
feel: **Relieved** for a moment, then **tired** of the same money treadmill.
S0.quote: Nothing radical changing isn't the same as nothing to worry about.
fieldNote: Her **money pressure** is already there before AI, with rent up and two weeks saved.
She frames everything through **management choices**, not technology itself.
Protective of an older colleague; **loyalty** to her team runs deep.
Overtime is the **fragile line** between coping and not coping.

steps.text: Push the union branch for guaranteed minimum hours in contracts
Set aside £20 a week into a separate savings pot
Keep leading the six-till front end and covering Saturday overtime

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I said about the self-checkouts: if they bring in machines, they owe the staff something back. Shorter weeks on the same pay, training, a say in it. I'd be posting that, and I'd be saying it to the store manager's face.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the tills go first, and I'm the tills. They're already halfway there with the self-checkouts. My job is mostly on my feet, so the robots taking longer gives me a few years, but the rota and ordering bits I do will go to software straight away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First I'd get every person on my team into the union, because twelve of us out of thirty isn't enough. I'd stop buying takeaways on Friday and put that money away. I'd ask about the customer service desk, because talking to angry people is the bit a machine is worst at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, mainly. There's only the one other supermarket in town, and it's smaller than ours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the rota and ordering would go to software. How much of your week is that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe five hours, doing the break plan and the cover sheet, plus chasing the bakery order. It's the part that makes me a team lead and not just a cashier. If an app does the rota, I'm a cashier on team-lead money, and the store will notice that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you'd never use AI tools. Would that change if the store trained you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they trained me in paid time, I'd sit through it. I wouldn't go home and learn it on my phone for free, though. I've given them enough free hours already.

say: If the store brings in **machines**, it owes staff **shorter weeks** on the same pay.
I'd tell the **store manager** directly that workers need a **say** in the change.
think: The **tills** go first, and the tills are most of **my job**.
Losing the **rota** and ordering work would make me a cashier on **team-lead pay**.
do: Sign up the **eighteen colleagues** who aren't yet in the **union**.
Cut the **Friday takeaway** and put that money into savings.
Ask to move onto the **customer service desk**, where people still want a person.
feel: **Anxious**, because there's only **one other supermarket** in town.
S1.quote: If an app does the rota, I'm a cashier on team-lead money, and the store will notice that.
fieldNote: She sees her **team-lead pay** resting on thinking tasks software could take.
Organising colleagues is her **first instinct**, before any personal plan.
Would only **learn AI** in paid time; she guards her unpaid hours.
Few local jobs make a move hard to picture.

steps.text: Recruit the eighteen non-members on her team into the union
Drop the Friday takeaway and bank the £25 instead
Apply for the customer service desk role at the same store

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need laws, not promises. If a company can replace a whole shop floor in five years, the government has to make them pay for it. I'd be at whatever rally the union called, with a placard, even though I hate crowds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really? I think I'd be out by about 2031, and Tom too, because his warehouse is the first place they'd put robots. The thinking AI in 2028 doesn't touch me much, but it kills the office jobs I'd have tried to move into. That's the bit that scares me: nowhere to jump.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start at the union branch the first week, pushing for redundancy terms while they still need us. I'd cancel the gym and the phone upgrade and squeeze our savings to maybe six weeks. And I'd talk to Tom about moving back in with my mum for a year to save the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly. I can picture the day the manager calls us all into the canteen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said both you and Tom could be out. What would you two actually say to each other that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tom would make a joke about starting a band. I'd do the sums on the back of a gas bill. Then we'd both go quiet, because neither of us has a plan B that pays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned moving back to your mum's. How would that go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum's got a box room and a lot of opinions. It'd save us six hundred a month, which is more than we've ever saved. I'd hate it, but I'd do it.

say: We need **laws**, not promises, when a firm can replace a **whole shop floor**.
I'd join any **union rally**, even though I really **hate crowds**.
think: I expect to be **out by 2031**, and my partner's warehouse job too.
Early **thinking AI** wipes out the **office jobs** I'd have moved into.
do: Push the union branch for **redundancy terms** while the store still needs staff.
Cancel the **gym and phone upgrade** to stretch savings to six weeks.
Move back into **Mum's box room** for a year to save **£600** a month.
feel: **Sick** at the thought of the canteen meeting where jobs get cut.
S2.quote: The thinking AI in 2028 doesn't touch me much, but it kills the office jobs I'd have tried to move into.
fieldNote: She sees the **three-year robot gap** as time with nowhere to go, not breathing room.
Two exposed earners in one household make this **doubly heavy**.
Her answer is **collective** first, family second, personal retraining barely at all.
The **gas-bill sums** show a planner without a cushion.

steps.text: Push the union branch for redundancy pay terms in the first week
Go to union rallies demanding a law on automation layoffs
Cancel the gym membership and phone upgrade
Move into her mum's box room for a year to save rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years to get this right, so start now. Shorter working week, a tax on the machines, money for retraining that's real money. I'd be the annoying one in the group chat sending petitions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think five years just means a slower version of the same ending. The robots for the tills land around 2034, so I'm thirty-five with no savings and a diploma in hospitality. The extra time helps if I do something with it, and I'm not good at doing something new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay on the union committee and push for a retraining fund in our contract. I'd look properly at a care course, because my mum says care homes always need people, and the college does evening classes. Tom and I would also put off getting a dog and a bigger flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tense. Less sick than the two-year one, but heavier for longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're not good at doing something new. What's held you back before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When they brought in the handheld scanners, I was the last one on my team to use them properly. I'm fine once I know a thing, but the learning bit makes me feel stupid. Care work is people, though, and people I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you want to hear from in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The government, with an actual plan, not a website. And the company, telling us the date instead of letting us find out from the papers. I'd take bad news early over nice words late.

say: Five years is time to get it right, with a **machine tax** and a shorter week.
I'd keep sending **petitions** around the group chat until people sign them.
think: Five years is a **slower version** of the same ending for cashiers.
By **2034** I'd be thirty-five with **no savings** and a hospitality diploma.
do: Push the union committee for a **retraining fund** written into our contract.
Look into **evening care courses** at the local college.
Put off getting a **dog** and moving to a **bigger flat**.
feel: **Tense**, less sick than the fast picture but **heavier for longer**.
S3.quote: I'd take bad news early over nice words late.
fieldNote: She knows extra time only helps if she uses it, and **doubts herself** there.
**Care work** appeals because it's about people, which she trusts herself with.
She wants honesty on **dates** from employers more than reassurance.
Family plans quietly pushed back.

steps.text: Push for a retraining fund in the store's union contract
Enrol in an evening care course at the local college
Put off the dog and the bigger flat with her partner Tom

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years means no excuses. Politicians can't say they didn't see it coming. I'd want every party asked what happens to shop workers in 2039, and I'd vote on that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years sounds like ages, and that worries me, because I know I'll leave it. I'll be thirty-seven when the robots are ready for the tills. I think I'd still have a job for most of that decade, which is more than most people get.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the care qualification over two years, evenings, while still on the tills. I'd keep pushing the union, but I'd also actually start the savings habit, even fifteen a week. And I'd stop pretending AI isn't real and let my niece show me the basics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but able to breathe. It's a long road, and I can see it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd let your niece show you AI. That's a change from earlier. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because ten years is too long to be stubborn. With two years, there's no point learning anything. With ten, being the one who won't learn is just daft.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you actually start, rather than leave it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A date on a letter. If the college course starts in September and I've paid the deposit, I'll go. If it's just an idea, I'll still be talking about it at forty.

say: Ten years means **no excuses** for politicians who say they didn't see it coming.
I'd **vote** on what each party plans for **shop workers** in 2039.
think: I worry I'll **leave it too late**, because ten years feels like ages.
I'd likely keep a **job on the tills** for most of the decade.
do: Study a **care qualification** over two years of evenings while still working.
Start saving **£15 a week**, however small it feels.
Let my **niece** show me the **basics of AI**.
feel: **Uneasy** but able to breathe, because she can see the road ahead.
S4.quote: With two years, there's no point learning anything. With ten, being the one who won't learn is just daft.
fieldNote: Longer warning softens her **resistance** to learning AI basics.
She knows she needs a **hard deadline**, like a paid deposit, to act.
Still expects tills to go by **2039**, so the worry doesn't disappear.
Votes on **shop-worker** policy above anything else.

steps.text: Pay the deposit on a two-year evening care qualification
Ask each local candidate what happens to shop workers by 2039
Save £15 a week in a pot she doesn't touch
Have her niece show her the basics of an AI chat tool

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, AGI by 2028, because it takes out Tom's warehouse and my tills in the same few years. What would help is the company telling us dates early and paying for training in work time. And a government that makes firms pay into a fund when they swap people for machines.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the customers. Some of our regulars come in mainly to talk to someone. Nobody's counting what happens to them when the tills are all screens.

headlineQuote: Some of our regulars come in mainly to talk to someone. Nobody's counting what happens to them when the tills are all screens.
portrait: Beth is a **27-year-old** till team lead in a mill-town supermarket, with two weeks of savings.
She's a lifelong **union member** who blames management choices, not machines, for lost hours.
She avoids **new technology** and only softens when she has ten years of warning.
Her household is **doubly exposed**, because her partner Tom works in a parcel warehouse.
Her mood moves from anxious under **AI Plateau** to alarmed when AGI arrives fast.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because her tills and Tom's **warehouse** job could both go within a few years.
whatWouldHelp: **Early dates** from the company and **paid training** in work time.
A **government fund** that firms pay into when they replace people with machines.
